findings.message: GLV feed: 1.31 mm² copper, TXL / GXL 125, k = 123 → withstand 26,079 A²s. That is 161 A for one second, or 1615 A for ten milliseconds.

The fuse clears first above 0 A, and the WIRE reaches its limit first below it. Below the crossover both times are long, so this is a thermal-overload question rather than a short-circuit one — but it means a sustained fault just under 0 A damages insulation while the fuse holds. Check that nothing in this circuit can stall at that current.

Above 40 A (4x rating) the fuse is energy-limited, so both curves fall as I^-2 and never cross again: it is one comparison of let-through 283 A²s against the wire's 26,079 A²s. The wire survives any fault current, however large.
The 0 A crossover lies outside the 2x–4x range your anchor points cover, so it is extrapolation rather than datasheet. Read one more point near 0.0x rating to place it on real data.
At 200 A the fuse clears in 7.1 ms, 92x inside the wire's 652.0 ms limit.

Observed spread sigma_ln = 0.019 (12 dof across 3 level(s)), itself uncertain by ±20%. Pass this into build_test_plan(log_scatter=...) and the next test is sized on these parts instead of on an assumption.
Measured curve: t = 39.7 x (I/I_rated)^-4.15 over 3 current levels.

Measured blow times differ from the declared curve by up to 100%, faster than the datasheet. Faster than published is safer for the wire and worse for nuisance trips; re-check inrush. Counterfeit or mislabelled blade fuses are common enough that this is the expected explanation, not an exotic one.

coarse.message: proof-of-concept (operator keypress, millis): timer resolution 500000 us, detection latency 281.2 ms, combined uncertainty ±165.0 ms. Shortest event measurable to 10% is 1650 ms.

Blocking serial output sits between the start and stop marks: 30 characters at 9600 baud is 31 ms added to every reading, in one direction only. Buffer the results and print after the test, not during it.

Blow detection is manual, so the 281 ms in this measurement is the operator's reaction time and not a property of the fuse. Every reading is biased long by roughly that much, and the bias is larger than most of the blow times worth measuring. Detect the current collapse on a shunt instead.
An expected blow time of 500.0 ms is dominated by the instrument: ±165.0 ms is 33% of it. Resolving this point to 5% needs detection at 40 Hz or faster.

plan_pct.message: Sized on an ASSUMED spread (sigma_ln = 0.30, module prior (not your fuses)), which nothing here has verified for the parts in your drawer. The count is quadratic in that assumption: if your fuses scatter half again as widely, this becomes 48 per level rather than 21. Run five at one current, pass them to refine_from_pilot(), and this stops being a guess.

4 current levels x 21 samples = 84 fuses (about 126 at 1.50 each) to pin the median blow time to ±14% at each level. 21 per level comes from the log-normal scatter of blow times, not from a round number — one fuse per level is an anecdote.
instrumented (shunt + ADC threshold, micros): timer resolution 1 us, detection latency 0.2 ms, combined uncertainty ±0.1 ms. Shortest event measurable to 10% is 1 ms.

finding.message: The pilot gives sigma_ln = 0.129 but only 1 degrees of freedom, so sigma is itself uncertain by ±71%. Sizing rigorously on the upper bound would demand 154352003 per level, which is not a real recommendation — it is the cost of not knowing sigma, not the cost of the scatter. Use the point estimate (3 per level) with that caveat, or spend 0 more fuses to reach a 9-sample pilot and get a bound worth acting on.

Pilot gives sigma_ln = 0.269 (10 dof, itself uncertain by ±22%). Sizing on the 0.430 upper bound rather than the point estimate costs 13 extra fuses per level and is what stops the test being under-sized half the time. Measured scatter is close to the prior; 22 per level against 11.
